items.title: Dacia Spring: Design Studio Explores Three Ways Forward
items.summary: The Dacia Spring has become one of Europe’s most important affordable EVs, proving that electric cars do not need huge batteries, enormous power outputs or premium prices to make sense. But deciding what replaces it could be considerably more complicated. Dacia now has the striking Hipster concept exploring an even smaller, more…
items.content_html:
The Dacia Spring has become one of Europe’s most important affordable EVs, proving that electric cars do not need huge batteries, enormous power outputs or premium prices to make sense. But deciding what replaces it could be considerably more complicated. Dacia now has the striking Hipster concept exploring an even smaller, more space-efficient approach, while parent company Renault is developing a growing portfolio of affordable electric cars and components that could potentially be shared across brands.

The most obvious route for the next Spring could be sitting within Renault’s own portfolio. The new Twingo E-Tech is built in Slovenia, giving Dacia access to a modern European-made EV base while avoiding the additional tariffs affecting Chinese-built electric cars. Sharing its underpinnings could also transform the Spring from an ultra-basic city car into something more comfortable, safer and better suited to journeys beyond urban limits.


Unlike today’s Spring, which traces its foundations back to the combustion-engined Renault Kwid, a Twingo-based replacement would start life as a purpose-built EV. That could bring meaningful improvements in packaging, refinement, safety and efficiency without abandoning the simplicity that makes the Spring appealing.

With Renault absorbing much of the underlying development work, Dacia could concentrate on delivering its own design and specification - potentially creating a considerably more mature electric car while keeping costs within reach of buyers who simply want affordable transport.


The Hipster concept itself is unlikely to reach production unchanged. Its near-vertical windscreen, extremely upright body and deliberately simple construction would create aerodynamic challenges at higher speeds, while its tiny footprint leaves limited space for the crash structures and safety technology expected of a modern production car. But the thinking behind it could be far more important than the concept itself.

A kei-car-inspired Spring could retain the Hipster’s focus on maximising interior space without following its dimensions quite so literally. By combining a short, narrow footprint with an upright cabin, clever EV packaging and a useful boot, Dacia could offer something increasingly rare: a genuinely tiny car that provides much of the everyday practicality of a larger hatchback, while remaining cheap to buy, run and park.


Around 20 years ago, Renault proved with the Modus that supermini underpinnings could be used to create something taller and considerably more space-efficient, prioritising passenger space and everyday practicality without the costs of moving to a larger platform. The idea arguably makes even more sense today. Compact electric motors and purpose-designed battery packaging give engineers opportunities that simply weren't available when the Modus was developed.

Applied intelligently, the same philosophy could create a remarkably spacious small EV with an exceptionally compact footprint. Rather than competing directly with Renault’s more conventional hatchbacks, a kei-inspired Spring could sit neatly at the bottom of the Renault Group ecosystem - simple, inexpensive and easy to park, but with enough usable space to work as a genuine everyday family car.


This version would make space the priority. Rather than following conventional supermini proportions, a kei-inspired Spring could use its height, upright body and compact EV hardware to maximise every millimetre of its footprint.

Positioned alongside small electric cars such as the Honda Super-N and Leapmotor T03, it could offer something genuinely different: Sandero-rivalling practicality within a much smaller, easier-to-park body. For buyers who value usable space above performance or styling trends, it could bring a new level of practicality per pound to the affordable EV market.


The third option is the simplest: don't fix what isn't broken. Renault has confirmed that the next Spring will be based on the new Twingo and built in Europe, but “Twingo-based” still leaves scope for extensive component sharing and cost-led engineering. Rather than reinventing the Spring completely, Renault Group could potentially retain elements of its proven low-cost Kwid-derived formula while incorporating newer Twingo-generation components, from batteries and motors to suspension technology.

Our Evolution design explores exactly that possibility: familiar Spring dimensions and straightforward engineering, modernised where it matters most. By concentrating investment on the components customers actually benefit from, Dacia could keep development costs down - and potentially keep the Spring exceptionally cheap to buy.

Dacia has never treated the Spring’s low price as something to apologise for. Instead, its exceptionally low price has become part of the car’s identity, and the formula has earned considerable praise for dramatically lowering the cost of entry into electric motoring. Today, the Fiat 500e, Citroën ë-C3, BYD Dolphin Surf, Honda Super-N and Leapmotor T03 can all be bought for under £20,000, yet the Spring starts at just £11,990.

There is no obvious single route for the next Spring. Sharing more with the Twingo could create a safer, more comfortable and capable small EV, while a Hipster-inspired approach could turn clever packaging into a new selling point, offering remarkable space within a genuinely tiny footprint. Alternatively, evolving today’s Kwid-derived formula could protect the quality that has made the Spring so disruptive in the first place: its price.

What matters is that Dacia doesn’t lose sight of what the Spring represents. As affordable EVs improve and prices continue to fall, simply making the next generation bigger, faster and more expensive would be the easy option. Keeping it genuinely accessible will be considerably harder - but potentially much more important. Whichever direction Dacia chooses, value should remain the Spring’s defining feature.

Image Credits: Concept renderings and design illustrations created by The New Yardstick Design Studio.

items.title: Jaguar's £100,000 Gamble: Why Its Reinvention Has No Room for Error
items.summary: Jaguar is preparing to launch arguably the most important car in its modern history. The production version of the Type 00 concept promises dramatic styling, enormous performance and a completely new direction for a brand that has spent years struggling to win sufficient market share against its premium rivals. Yet the car…
items.content_html:
Jaguar is preparing to launch arguably the most important car in its modern history. The production version of the Type 00 concept promises dramatic styling, enormous performance and a completely new direction for a brand that has spent years struggling to win sufficient market share against its premium rivals.

Yet the car itself may prove to be the easy part. Jaguar’s controversial reinvention generated extraordinary attention long before customers had a new model to buy, while its move further upmarket places it increasingly close to Range Rover and Defender territory.

It is nearly 20 years since Jaguar began its last major reinvention. The transformation started with the impressively successful XF, developed under Ford before Tata took control in 2008. The striking X351 XJ soon followed, becoming an important halo model, while the F-Type was the first all-new Jaguar developed entirely under Tata ownership. In other words, Jaguar’s current owners have had plenty of time to understand what the brand represents.

From the rear, Jaguar’s new direction arguably makes even more sense. The long, sweeping body, enormous bonnet and glassless tail give the 001 genuine GT character, while avoiding the increasingly generic fastback shape adopted by many large EVs. As a spiritual successor to the XJ, it is dramatic, distinctive and unmistakably expensive - exactly what a flagship Jaguar should be.

The way Jaguar chose to introduce this new era was considerably harder to admire. Its infamous launch campaign was deliberately provocative, and subsequent surprise at the backlash was never particularly convincing. This was a calculated PR exercise designed to make people talk about Jaguar - and it worked. But deliberately distancing a brand from parts of its existing audience remains an enormous gamble, however successful the publicity.

While we don't yet know exactly how much of the Type 00's exterior will survive into production, Jaguar has already given us a surprisingly clear look inside - and the cabin appears hugely promising. Its clean design has a strong technology focus, yet everything we've seen so far looks fresh, expensive and thoughtfully resolved throughout.

The small central control screen almost resembles a smartphone, but that isn't necessarily a criticism. Smartphones have spent years refining interfaces that millions of us instinctively understand, and Jaguar appears to have embraced that familiarity rather than reinventing it for the sake of being different. The large display behind the steering wheel also looks perfectly positioned within the driver's natural line of sight.

However successful the 001 proves, Jaguar will eventually need more than a low-volume electric GT to rebuild a sustainable global business. A crossover or SUV therefore seems difficult to avoid, potentially giving the brand access to far more customers. Our rendering imagines how that could look - lower and more elegant than a traditional Land Rover, but unmistakably related to Jaguar’s new design direction.

The harder question is where JLR would put it. The old F-Pace occupied relatively straightforward territory below the Range Rover Sport, but a new Jaguar competing around £100,000 would arrive in a considerably more crowded family. Range Rover continues to push further into luxury, while Defender has expanded into an increasingly desirable and expensive brand of its own. Add a new Jaguar crossover and JLR risks winning customers from itself rather than its competitors.

Jaguar isn't the only unresolved part of the House of Brands strategy either. Discovery has now gone a decade without a genuinely new generation, while Defender's success has increasingly occupied territory that once belonged naturally to it. Creating greater separation may require Range Rover and Defender to move further upmarket - potentially squeezing the very space Jaguar now wants to enter.

None of this means Jaguar's reinvention cannot work. In fact, the 001 increasingly looks like it could become one of the most distinctive luxury cars on sale. But building a desirable car and rebuilding a sustainable brand are very different challenges. Jaguar now needs the right balance of performance, range, efficiency, pricing and eventually volume - while JLR must prove that four increasingly ambitious brands can grow alongside one another without simply moving the same customers between badges.

The 001 may show us whether the new Jaguar can build a great car. What comes after it will show whether JLR has built a great strategy.

Image Credits: Jaguar XJ and interior imagery © Jaguar Land Rover (JLR). Concept renderings created by The New Yardstick Design Studio.

items.title: Three Cars, One Mission: Peugeot's Bold New Premium Small Car Strategy
items.summary: Twenty years ago, Peugeot offered one of Europe's broadest B-segment line-ups, with hatchbacks, estates, convertibles, people carriers and overlapping generations all competing for buyers. Today, just the 208 and 2008 remain. However, that could soon change. Growing evidence from Peugeot's product roadmap and Stellantis' wider platform strategy suggests the French manufacturer could…
items.content_html:
Peugeot's decision to simplify its small car range has proved remarkably successful. Around two decades ago, the brand offered an extraordinary 12 different B-segment body styles, ranging from three- and five-door hatchbacks to estates, convertibles and compact people carriers. Today, that choice has been distilled down to just the 208 and 2008, yet Peugeot has retained one of Europe's leading positions in the segment.


Replacing diesel with efficient 48-volt hybrid powertrains has helped keep the range competitive as buyer preferences have evolved. At the same time, Peugeot's 2023 updates introduced refreshed styling, upgraded technology and improved electric powertrains, with WLTP ranges for both the E-208 and E-2008 increasing to around 260 miles.

Combined with increasingly premium interiors, stronger pricing and the manufacturing efficiencies available through Stellantis, Peugeot now finds itself in a far stronger financial position than it did during the early 2010s. That raises an interesting question: rather than replacing both models outright, could Peugeot now afford to expand choice once again?

If reports prove accurate, the next-generation Peugeot E-208 will become the first production model to showcase Stellantis' dedicated STLA Small architecture. Unlike today's multi-energy platform, which has gradually reached its limits, the new EV-only chassis has been engineered from the outset around electric power, allowing significantly larger battery packs, improved efficiency and faster charging.

Rather than chasing outright class records, Peugeot is likely to position the E-208 just below the limits of what STLA Small can offer. A line-up centred around approximately 58kWh and 73kWh usable battery options would comfortably cover everything from everyday commuting to long-distance family use, with flagship versions capable of around 350 miles of WLTP range while remaining competitively priced. Above it, Alfa Romeo and DS Automobiles would still have room to justify larger batteries, more powerful drivetrains and additional luxury features.


The result should be a small car that continues Peugeot's journey further upmarket. A new-generation i-Cockpit, faster infotainment, improved driver assistance systems and styling inspired by Peugeot's striking Polygon concept would build on the strengths of today's model, reinforcing the brand's increasingly premium positioning without abandoning the value that has helped make the current 208 one of Europe's best-selling superminis.


The next-generation E-208 won't just introduce a new electric platform – it could also mark the beginning of Peugeot's most radical interior evolution yet. Building on the success of the award-winning i-Cockpit, the new model is expected to adopt the brand's latest digital architecture, centred around the futuristic Hypersquare steer-by-wire controller.

Removing the mechanical connection between steering wheel and front wheels allows a more compact driving position, greater cabin flexibility and a cleaner dashboard design. Combined with faster software, richer graphics and improved driver assistance technology, the next E-208 could push Peugeot's premium ambitions even further while showcasing the innovation Stellantis is investing in its next generation of electric vehicles.


While an all-new electric E-208 could become Peugeot's technological flagship, the current-generation 208 still has plenty to offer. Remaining one of Europe's best-selling superminis around six years after its UK launch, the model continues to prove that strong design, impressive quality and well-judged engineering can extend a vehicle's lifespan far beyond the industry norm.

Rather than replacing a winning formula, Peugeot could instead allow the current car to continue alongside its electric successor, giving buyers the choice of efficient petrol and hybrid power without the compromises often associated with multi-energy platforms.


Under the bonnet, Peugeot would have little reason to reinvent the recipe. The latest 110hp and 145hp 48-volt Hybrid powertrains already rank among the strongest in the class, combining brisk performance with excellent fuel economy and lower emissions. Entry-level versions are also expected to benefit from Stellantis' updated 98hp 1.2-litre petrol engine, replacing the earlier wet timing belt with the more durable timing chain design already adopted by the hybrid models.

Combined with a second exterior facelift, subtle cabin improvements and continued competitive pricing, the 208 could remain one of Europe's strongest premium small cars while complementing, rather than competing with, the all-new STLA Small E-208.


The 2008 has quietly become one of Peugeot's biggest success stories. Combining SUV styling with family-friendly practicality, a high-quality interior and competitive pricing, it continues to attract buyers across Europe despite approaching the latter half of its lifecycle.

With no immediate replacement expected, a second facelift would allow Peugeot to keep one of its strongest-selling models fresh while continuing to offer buyers the choice of efficient petrol, hybrid and electric powertrains within a proven package.

Unlike the 208, the 2008 has little need for a dramatic change in direction. Its spacious 434-litre boot, comfortable ride, premium cabin and efficient range of petrol, hybrid and electric powertrains already make it one of the strongest all-round compact SUVs on sale.

Buyers needing greater electric range can simply step up to the larger 3008, where 73kWh and 98kWh battery options deliver up to 440 miles of WLTP range, leaving the 2008 free to continue focusing on affordability, efficiency and everyday usability.

If Peugeot does adopt this three-car strategy, it wouldn't be expanding its line-up for the sake of it. Instead, each model would have a clearly defined role, allowing the brand to offer greater choice while building on the success of three already highly competitive products.

Image credits: The New Yardstick concept renderings, created using original digital artwork inspired by Peugeot design language. Peugeot trademarks and badges remain the property of Peugeot / Stellantis and are used for illustrative editorial purposes only.

items.title: The Best Value Pre-Registered Vans on Sale Right Now
items.summary: Pre-registered vans continue to offer some of the biggest savings anywhere in the UK new vehicle market, with discounts often reaching tens of thousands of pounds compared with official list prices. Whether you're a business owner, sole trader or private buyer, these nearly-new vehicles can deliver exceptional value without the compromises of…
items.content_html:
Pre-registered vans continue to offer some of the biggest savings anywhere in the UK new vehicle market, with discounts often reaching tens of thousands of pounds compared with official list prices.

Whether you're a business owner, sole trader or private buyer, these nearly-new vehicles can deliver exceptional value without the compromises of buying an older used van.

From compact electric city vans to heavy-duty long-wheelbase workhorses, we've highlighted some of the best pre-registered commercial vehicle deals currently available, comparing official RRPs with typical market prices to show where the biggest savings can be found.


Citroën ë-C3 Van
RRP From : £17,535 + VAT (£21,042 inc. VAT)
Pre Reg From : c. £13,250 + VAT (£15,900 inc. VAT)

The Citroën ë-C3 Van brings SUV-inspired styling and electric efficiency to the compact van market at an exceptionally competitive price. Despite its compact dimensions, it offers a practical load area and a comfortable driving experience, making it well suited to urban businesses and local deliveries.

Dacia Spring Cargo
RRP From : £13,995 + VAT (£16,794 inc. VAT)
Pre Reg From : c. £7,995 + VAT (£9,594 inc. VAT)

The Dacia Spring Cargo strips electric van ownership back to the essentials, offering compact dimensions, low running costs and remarkable value. While its modest performance and payload mean it won't suit every business, it's ideal for urban deliveries and local trades.

At typical pre-registered prices, it costs around the same as many five-year-old compact diesel vans, making it one of the cheapest ways to own a brand-new electric commercial vehicle. For businesses that don't need a large van, the Spring Cargo proves that switching to electric can be surprisingly affordable.


Farizon SV
RRP From : £40,000 + VAT (£48,000 inc. VAT)
Pre-Reg Price : c. £24,990 + VAT (£29,988 inc. VAT)

The Farizon SV is one of the most convincing new entrants to the UK electric van market, combining a dedicated EV platform with impressive practicality, refinement and payload capacity. Unlike many rivals adapted from diesel-powered vans, it has been designed as an electric vehicle from the outset, helping maximise efficiency and interior space.

The largest 83kWh battery delivers up to 234 miles of WLTP range, around 17 miles further than the comparable 75kWh Vauxhall Vivaro Electric. Strong refinement, modern technology and competitive operating costs make the Farizon SV a compelling alternative to more established medium electric vans.


Fiat Ducato
RRP From : £35,260 + VAT (£42,312 inc. VAT)
Pre Reg From : c. £22,490 + VAT (£26,988 inc. VAT)

The Fiat Ducato has long been one of Europe's most successful large vans, offering an enormous choice of body lengths, roof heights and bodystyles, including panel vans, chassis cabs, tippers, curtain-siders and Lutons. Designed for demanding commercial use, it combines impressive payloads with proven diesel engines, while the latest E-Ducato offers up to 263 miles of WLTP range.

Its class-leading width between the rear wheel arches makes it a favourite for motorhome conversions, allowing transverse fixed beds, while its versatility ensures it remains one of the UK's hardest-working large vans.

Ford Transit Courier
RRP From : £17,800 + VAT (£21,360 inc. VAT)
Pre Reg From : c. £15,990 + VAT (£19,188 inc. VAT)

The Ford Transit Courier combines compact dimensions with one of the boldest designs in Ford's commercial vehicle range, giving it rugged SUV-inspired styling and excellent proportions. Despite its small footprint, it offers an impressive load area that's ideal for urban deliveries and local trades.

Buyers can choose between Ford's economical 1.0-litre EcoBoost petrol engine or a fully electric version, with surprisingly little price difference between the two on the pre-registered market. Comfortable, easy to drive and highly practical, the Transit Courier proves that a compact van doesn't have to compromise on capability or everyday usability.


Iveco Daily
RRP From : £35,260 + VAT (£42,312 inc. VAT)
Pre Reg From : c. £28,995 + VAT (£34,794 inc. VAT)

The Iveco Daily is built for the toughest jobs, using a traditional body-on-frame chassis that allows it to carry heavier payloads and tackle more demanding work than many monocoque rivals. Available in an enormous range of body lengths, wheelbases and bodystyles, it includes some of the largest panel vans available in the UK.

While often costing more than many competitors, its truck-inspired construction, durability and exceptional versatility make it a favourite with operators carrying heavy loads every day.


Kia PV5 Cargo
RRP From : £27,645 + VAT (£33,174 inc. VAT)
Pre Reg From : c. £21,495 + VAT (£25,794 inc. VAT)

The Kia PV5 Cargo brings fresh thinking to the medium van market, sacrificing a little outright load space in favour of distinctive styling, modern technology and a dedicated electric platform. Kia has got the design right, creating one of the most attractive commercial vehicles currently on sale.

Standard-range models already offer impressive value, while spending around £2,500 more on the pre-registered market unlocks the Long Range version, increasing WLTP range to an impressive 258 miles. With a practical load area, comfortable cabin and Kia's seven-year warranty, the PV5 is a compelling alternative to more established electric vans. 


Mercedes-Benz eCitan
RRP From : £29,695 + VAT (£35,634 inc. VAT)
Pre Reg From : c. £17,995 + VAT (£21,594 inc. VAT)

The Mercedes-Benz eCitan proves that a premium badge doesn't have to come with a premium price tag. Typical pre-registered examples undercut the equivalent ICE Citan by around £1,000, making the electric version the more compelling buy.

A WLTP range of up to 175 miles is more than sufficient for last-mile deliveries, urban businesses and local trades, while the refined driving experience and high-quality cabin help justify the Mercedes-Benz badge. For buyers seeking premium appeal without stretching their budget, the eCitan stands out as one of the most convincing small electric van bargains currently available.


Nissan Townstar
RRP From : £22,640 + VAT (£27,168 inc. VAT)
Pre Reg From : c. £15,098 + VAT (£18,118 inc. VAT)


Peugeot E-Expert
RRP From : £28,905 + VAT (£34,686 inc. VAT)
Pre Reg From : c. £16,994 + VAT (£20,393 inc. VAT)

The Peugeot E-Expert proves that switching to an electric medium van no longer requires a premium budget. Typical pre-registered examples undercut equivalent diesel models by around £1,000, giving buyers zero-emission driving for less money.

Offering medium van practicality at little more than the price of many compact vans, the E-Expert combines a modern, high-tech cabin with a sharper facelifted design that gives it a more desirable appearance. A WLTP range of up to 217 miles comfortably covers the needs of many businesses, making the E-Expert one of the strongest value electric van deals currently available.


Renault Trafic E-Tech
RRP From : £39,500 + VAT (£47,400 inc. VAT)
Pre Reg From : c. £15,000 + VAT (£18,000 inc. VAT)

The Renault Trafic E-Tech is one of the best-value electric vans on the pre-registered market, with discounts of well over £20,000 from its original list price. It also undercuts the equivalent diesel model by almost £5,000, making the switch to electric an easy financial decision for many buyers.

A WLTP range of up to 183 miles comfortably covers typical business needs, while its load area remains one of the largest in the medium van sector, where many newer rivals have become slightly smaller.


Toyota Corolla Commercial
RRP From : £23,961.67 + VAT (£28,754 inc. VAT)
Pre-Reg Price : c. £17,992 + VAT (£21,590 inc. VAT)

The Corolla Commercial proves that a practical van doesn't need to sacrifice the comfort and efficiency of a passenger car. Based on the Corolla Touring Sports estate, which starts from £31,560, it combines Toyota's proven self-charging hybrid system with excellent fuel economy and a refined driving experience.

Toyota now offers an impressive six-model commercial vehicle range in the UK, while the Corolla Commercial provides a unique alternative to traditional small vans, blending car-like comfort with outstanding reliability and low running costs.


Vauxhall Combo
RRP From : £22,870 + VAT (£27,444 inc. VAT)
Pre Reg From : c. £13,995 + VAT (£16,794 inc. VAT)


Volkswagen Caddy
RRP From : £25,825 + VAT (£30,990 inc. VAT)
Pre Reg From : c. £20,198 + VAT (£24,238 inc. VAT)

The Volkswagen Caddy combines car-like comfort, impressive refinement and a premium cabin with the practicality expected of a compact van. Closely related to the Ford Transit Connect, it is available with efficient diesel engines or a plug-in hybrid, with the latter typically costing around £2,500 more on the pre-registered market.

While not the cheapest option in its class, strong pre-registered discounts significantly reduce the premium often associated with German brands. For buyers seeking comfort, technology and a prestigious badge, the Caddy is now a far more convincing proposition.

Prices, specifications and availability were correct at the time of publication but may change without notice. Manufacturer recommended retail prices (RRPs) are shown excluding VAT, with VAT-inclusive prices provided for guidance at the current UK rate of 20%. Typical pre-registered prices are approximate UK market values and may vary depending on specification, location, seller and VAT status. Unless otherwise stated, vehicle images are official manufacturer press photographs and remain the copyright of their respective manufacturers.

items.title: 2027 Lexus UX Concept: More Space, More Choice, Same Lexus Quality
items.summary: The current Lexus UX has been one of the brand's most distinctive models, combining premium quality, refined hybrid power and Lexus' renowned reliability in a compact SUV. However, having been on sale in the UK since 2019, it is now the oldest passenger car in the Lexus range, and its age is…
items.content_html:
The current Lexus UX has been one of the brand's most distinctive models, combining premium quality, refined hybrid power and Lexus' renowned reliability in a compact SUV. However, having been on sale in the UK since 2019, it is now the oldest passenger car in the Lexus range, and its age is beginning to show.

Despite sitting above the newer LBX, the UX actually offers less passenger and boot space, while the compact premium SUV segment has continued to move forwards.


Despite measuring over 300mm longer than the LBX, the current UX offers just 320 litres of boot space, compared with the smaller SUV's 402 litres. That places the UX towards the bottom of the premium compact SUV class for outright practicality, despite its larger footprint.

The next-generation model doesn't need to sacrifice its sleek, coupe-inspired stance to address this. SUVs such as the Renault Austral and Peugeot 3008 demonstrate that a stylish 4.5-metre family SUV can comfortably offer more than 500 litres of luggage space without losing its dynamic proportions.


Toyota and Lexus have earned an outstanding reputation for build quality, reliability and intuitive ergonomics, and that's a philosophy we've carried into our 2027 UX concept. Inspired by the clean, horizontal dashboard of the latest Lexus ES, the cabin has been reworked with proportions better suited to a C-segment SUV, creating a greater sense of width and space.


While Lexus has moved away from traditional high-performance petrol models, the brand already has the ingredients to create a compelling modern F flagship. Using the existing 366hp 2.4-litre turbocharged hybrid powertrain from the RX, a Lexus UX F could deliver effortless all-weather performance without abandoning the efficiency expected of a modern Lexus.


A next-generation Lexus UX doesn't need to reinvent the formula to become one of the most complete contenders in the premium compact SUV class.

Toyota and Lexus already offer a range of proven electrified powertrains that could naturally suit the model, from an efficient 2.5-litre self-charging hybrid and a more powerful plug-in hybrid, to a fully electric 77kWh version and even a 366hp performance-focused F flagship.

Combined with a more spacious interior, a significantly larger boot and a fresh interpretation of Lexus' evolving design language, the result could build on the current UX's strengths while addressing its biggest weaknesses.

By combining quality, reliability, efficiency and improved practicality, Lexus has the opportunity to create a compact SUV capable of competing with the very best in the segment.

(Image Credits: The New Yardstick)

items.title: Dacia Bigster Not Big Enough? 6 Bigger SUVs for Under £30,000 Pre-Registered
items.summary: The Dacia Bigster is one of the largest family SUVs available for under £30,000, offering exceptional value and one of the biggest boots in its class. However, every manufacturer packages its interior differently. (Image Credits: Dacia) The Bigster makes excellent use of its footprint by prioritising luggage space, meaning rear passenger accommodation…
items.content_html:
The Dacia Bigster is one of the largest family SUVs available for under £30,000, offering exceptional value and one of the biggest boots in its class. However, every manufacturer packages its interior differently. (Image Credits: Dacia)

The Bigster makes excellent use of its footprint by prioritising luggage space, meaning rear passenger accommodation is good rather than class-leading, while some rivals use their larger footprints to offer roomier second-row seating, seven-seat versatility or space for plug-in hybrid and fully electric powertrains.

If you regularly carry adult passengers or simply want an even bigger family SUV, the six alternatives below are all available for under £30,000 pre-registered.


Chery Tiggo 8
Starting from around £24,500 pre-registered, the Chery Tiggo 8 offers an impressive amount of SUV for the money. Measuring 4,725mm long, it's significantly larger than the Dacia Bigster and comes with seven seats as standard, making it a practical choice for growing families or anyone needing occasional extra passenger space. (Image Credits: Chery)

While its 494-litre boot with the third row folded is typical of many seven-seat SUVs, it's a more impressive achievement when you consider the Tiggo 8 also packages a plug-in hybrid powertrain beneath the bodywork.

Combined with generous standard equipment, a modern interior and the potential for low running costs, it makes a compelling alternative for buyers wanting maximum versatility without spending more than £30,000 pre-registered.


Citroën C5 Aircross
Available from around £25,000 pre-registered, the Citroën C5 Aircross is slightly larger than the Dacia Bigster, measuring 4,652mm long. Rather than using that extra length to maximise boot capacity, Citroën has prioritised passenger comfort, with generous rear legroom, a spacious second row and one of the most comfortable rides in the family SUV class. (Image Credits: Citroën)

Buyers can choose from an economical 145hp mild hybrid, a plug-in hybrid or a fully electric Long Range model capable of travelling up to 421 miles on a full charge.


KGM Torres
Available from around £27,000 pre-registered, the KGM Torres is one of the most overlooked large family SUVs on sale. Measuring 4,705mm long, it's comfortably larger than the Dacia Bigster and combines bold styling with a surprisingly plush interior that feels a step above many mainstream rivals. (Image Credits: KGM)

Buyers can choose between a full hybrid or fully electric powertrain, both offering generous boot space without compromising practicality. Despite competing in one of the UK's busiest SUV segments, the Torres remains a rare sight on British roads, meaning it still turns heads wherever it goes.


Leapmotor C10
Available for under £30,000 pre-registered, the Leapmotor C10 is one of the most spacious electric family SUVs available for the money, measuring 4,739mm long. While its 435-litre boot is smaller than the Dacia Bigster's, it's still easily large enough for everyday family life, with the C10 instead using its long 2,825mm wheelbase to maximise rear passenger space and create an impressively airy cabin. (Image Credits: Leapmotor)


Nissan X-Trail
Available from around £26,000 pre-registered, the Nissan X-Trail is often overlooked alongside the hugely successful Qashqai, yet it offers significantly more space and practicality for growing families. (Image Credits: Nissan)

Measuring 4,680mm long, buyers can choose from Nissan's efficient e-POWER hybrid or the e-4ORCE four-wheel drive version, both combining low running costs with a smooth, refined driving experience. A generous boot, available seven-seat layout and smart, modern styling make the X-Trail an excellent step up for buyers who have outgrown a Qashqai.


Skywell BE11
Available for under £15,000 pre-registered, the Skywell BE11 is comfortably the cheapest SUV featured here and represents remarkable value for buyers prioritising space over badge appeal. Measuring 4,720mm long, it offers an exceptionally roomy cabin with generous rear legroom, a practical family-friendly interior and a generous equipment list that includes many features usually found on far more expensive SUVs. (Image Credits: Skywell)

While its styling won't appeal to everyone and early reviews criticised its driving dynamics and infotainment, the BE11 still looks more than capable of handling everyday family duties. If your priorities are maximum space for minimum money, it's difficult to think of another large electric SUV that offers so much for so little.

The Dacia Bigster remains one of the best-value large family SUVs you can buy brand new, offering impressive space, practicality and low running costs at a price few rivals can match. However, the pre-registered market changes the playing field dramatically.

For similar money, buyers can choose from a range of larger, more established and increasingly talented SUVs, many offering seven seats, electric or plug-in powertrains, plus even greater passenger space and equipment. As always, the best choice depends on your priorities, but it certainly pays to look beyond the obvious options.

items.title: Could These Two Models Complete Suzuki's Future Line-up?
items.summary: Suzuki's range has become one of the simplest on sale, but two clear opportunities remain. At the bottom sits the biggest omission of all: there's no modern successor to cars like the Alto, Celerio or Ignis. An affordable city car has long been one of Suzuki's greatest strengths, and an electric replacement…
items.content_html:
Suzuki's range has become one of the simplest on sale, but two clear opportunities remain. At the bottom sits the biggest omission of all: there's no modern successor to cars like the Alto, Celerio or Ignis.

An affordable city car has long been one of Suzuki's greatest strengths, and an electric replacement could not only restore that missing rung of the ladder, but also help the brand meet increasingly demanding European emissions regulations.

Meanwhile, the Vitara and S-Cross are beginning to show their age. Replacing both with a single new hybrid SUV would create a more logical bridge between the e Vitara and Across.


The Japanese-market e-Sky demonstrates how Suzuki could return to the kei car segment, but Europe presents a different challenge. Rather than starting again, Suzuki could adapt the same design into a slightly larger global model, preserving its compact footprint while improving refinement, luggage space and everyday usability.


A modest electric motor wouldn't be a compromise – it would be entirely in keeping with Suzuki's philosophy. The Alto, Celerio and Ignis were never bought for their performance, but for their dependability, low running costs and ability to make the most of every centimetre of road and parking space.


Higher up the range, Suzuki faces a different challenge. The Vitara and S-Cross have served the brand well, but after years on sale the two SUVs have become increasingly similar in size and purpose. With the all-electric e Vitara now covering buyers ready to make the switch to EVs, Suzuki has an opportunity to simplify its line-up.

Replacing both models with a single hybrid-only S-Cross would reduce complexity and create a clearer choice for customers.

Growing to around 4.4 metres long, the new S-Cross would become Suzuki's mainstay family SUV. Positioned below the larger plug-in hybrid Across, which would continue to rival cars such as the Nissan X-Trail and Vauxhall Grandland, it would instead target the heart of the market alongside the Nissan Qashqai and Vauxhall Frontera.

The result would be a simpler, more clearly defined SUV range, with each model occupying its own distinct role. Taken together, the e-Sky and new S-Cross show how Suzuki could strengthen its line-up without abandoning the qualities that have defined the brand for decades.

Compact dimensions, sensible engineering and dependable value would remain at the heart of every model, creating a range that feels more complete, more logical and better prepared for the years ahead.


(Image Credits: The New Yardstick)

items.title: 8 Brilliant 50mpg City Cars You Can Buy for Around £3,000
items.summary: With the average price of a new car now well beyond the reach of many households, a dependable used city car makes more sense than ever. Whether you're looking for an affordable first car, a low-cost commuter or a second vehicle to keep everyday running costs down, spending around £3,000 can still…
items.content_html:
With the average price of a new car now well beyond the reach of many households, a dependable used city car makes more sense than ever. Whether you're looking for an affordable first car, a low-cost commuter or a second vehicle to keep everyday running costs down, spending around £3,000 can still buy something economical, reliable and genuinely enjoyable to own.

For this list, we've focused on cars capable of returning around 50mpg in everyday driving, while keeping road tax, servicing and insurance comfortably affordable. Practicality, reliability and parts availability all played a major role too, because an inexpensive car can quickly become an expensive mistake if it spends more time in the garage than on the road.

From cleverly packaged family favourites to stylish urban runabouts, these eight city cars continue to prove that sensible motoring doesn't have to mean sacrificing character or quality.


The Citroën C1 proves that simple engineering often makes for the smartest used buy. Developed alongside the Toyota Aygo and Peugeot 107/108, it shares Toyota's dependable 1.0-litre petrol engine, giving owners excellent reliability, impressive fuel economy and low running costs.

A budget of around £3,000 should buy a well-maintained 2015 example with roughly 70,000 miles, while real-world fuel economy of 55–58mpg is easily achievable. Well-equipped Flair models even offer a touchscreen with Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, making the cabin feel surprisingly modern for the money.

Its compact size makes parking effortless, while servicing, tyres and replacement parts remain refreshingly affordable. The boot is on the small side and, like its Toyota and Peugeot siblings, the C1 is strictly a four-seater, but as an inexpensive city car it remains one of the strongest all-round buys available for around £3,000.


The Fiat Panda proves that practicality doesn't have to come in a large package. Its tall, boxy design creates a surprisingly spacious cabin with excellent headroom and one of the most usable interiors in the city car class, while its unmistakable Italian styling gives it a charm few rivals can match.

A budget of around £3,000 should buy a well-maintained 2016 1.2-litre petrol model with roughly 70,000 miles, although the same money can also secure 4x4, diesel and TwinAir versions. The naturally aspirated petrol engines are dependable, inexpensive to maintain and capable of around 50–55mpg in everyday driving.

The charismatic TwinAir is great fun but rarely delivers its ambitious official fuel economy figures, while road noise is more noticeable than in larger hatchbacks. For buyers wanting maximum space and personality for minimal money, the Panda remains one of the most likeable small cars on the road.

The Hyundai i10 takes a refreshingly sensible approach to city car motoring, prioritising solid build quality, practicality and reliability over fashionable styling or gimmicky features. Its roomy cabin comfortably accommodates four adults, while the upright design makes it feel larger inside than its compact dimensions suggest.

A budget of around £3,000 should buy a 2014 example of the newer generation with roughly 90,000 miles, while buyers wanting lower mileage may need to consider the older, slightly awkwardly proportioned first-generation model instead.

The dependable 1.2-litre petrol engine typically returns 46–50mpg in everyday driving and is inexpensive to maintain. It may not have the quirky personality of a Fiat Panda or Citroën C1, but as an honest, dependable small car that's built to last, the i10 remains one of the safest used buys in its class.


The third-generation Renault Twingo stands out from almost every other city car thanks to its unusual rear-engine, rear-wheel-drive layout. For most buyers, the dependable 1.0-litre petrol is the sensible choice, returning a realistic 50–56mpg while keeping running costs reassuringly low.

However, the punchier 0.9 TCe turbo is well worth considering if you want to make the most of the Twingo's unique character, adding genuinely enjoyable performance that can put a smile on your face every time you drive. With no engine under the bonnet, Renault was also able to engineer an exceptionally tight turning circle, making the Twingo brilliantly manoeuvrable around town.

A budget of around £3,000 should buy a 2015 example with roughly 80,000 miles. The rear-engine layout does reduce boot space compared with most rivals, but it's a small price to pay for such a distinctive and enjoyable city car.

The SEAT Mii shares its foundations with the Volkswagen Up and Škoda Citigo, combining clever packaging with reassuringly low running costs. There's space for four adults, a usefully shaped boot and excellent all-round visibility, while the large windows make it particularly easy to park and thread through busy streets.

Expect 45–50mpg from the dependable petrol engines, with plentiful parts helping to keep servicing and repairs affordable. While some rivals are quicker or slightly more economical, few feel quite as easy and confidence-inspiring to drive every day.

A budget of around £3,000 should buy a 2014 example with roughly 70,000 miles, making the Mii one of the most practical and sensible city cars available at this price.


The Suzuki Celerio is one of the most underrated city cars on the used market. It won't win awards for cutting-edge technology or eye-catching styling, but it makes up for both with outstanding reliability, low running costs and impressive practicality.

Its tall, upright design won't appeal to everyone, yet it creates generous headroom for four adults and a surprisingly useful boot that becomes even more versatile with the rear seats folded. The dependable 1.0-litre petrol engine is capable of an impressive 50–58mpg in everyday driving, helping to keep fuel bills reassuringly low.

A budget of around £3,000 should buy a 2016 example with roughly 70,000 miles, making the Celerio an excellent choice for buyers who value substance over style.


The Suzuki Ignis brings something genuinely different to the city car market, blending compact dimensions with chunky SUV-inspired styling that has made it a favourite among buyers wanting something with a little more character. It isn't quite as spacious as the Suzuki Celerio, but it's every bit as dependable while remaining inexpensive to run.

The reliable 1.2-litre petrol engine comfortably returns 50–58mpg in everyday driving, while later mild hybrid models can achieve 60mpg or more. Unusually for a car of this size, selected models are even available with ALLGRIP four-wheel drive, adding extra confidence on muddy lanes and winter roads.

A £3,000 budget is ambitious, but early higher-mileage examples are beginning to fall within reach, giving buyers an appealing and distinctive alternative to more conventional city cars.


The Vauxhall Adam brought a fresh sense of style to the city car market, taking direct aim at the Fiat 500 with an enormous choice of colours, roof designs and interior trims. Buyers searching the used market will quickly discover that no two Adams seem quite the same, so it's worth taking time to compare specifications carefully.

The dependable 1.2 and 1.4-litre naturally aspirated petrol engines remain the safest choices, while the later 1.0-litre turbo combines impressive performance with excellent fuel economy. Stretch your budget beyond £5,000 and you'll find the rugged Adam Rocks, complete with SUV-inspired body cladding, or the Rocks Air, which adds a full-length folding canvas roof.

The range is topped by the rapid 150hp Adam S, a surprisingly quick hot hatch that combines strong turbocharged performance with superb Recaro sports seats and remains one of the used market's best-kept secrets.

A budget of around £3,000 should buy a 2015 example with roughly 80,000 miles, although the Adam's vast number of trims and options means careful shopping is essential.

There's no single "best" city car for £3,000 because every buyer has different priorities. If reliability and low running costs matter most, cars like the Citroën C1, Hyundai i10 and Suzuki Celerio are difficult to fault. Those wanting more character may prefer the Fiat Panda, Renault Twingo or Vauxhall Adam, while the Suzuki Ignis offers a distinctive crossover alternative.

Whichever you choose, £3,000 remains one of the sweetest spots in today's used market, buying cars that are economical to run, inexpensive to maintain and, with a little careful shopping, capable of providing many more years of dependable motoring.

Prices, mileages and fuel economy are based on the UK used market in July 2026 and will vary depending on condition, specification and location. Unless otherwise stated, vehicle images are manufacturer press photographs and remain the copyright of their respective manufacturers.

items.title: Alpine A190: The Affordable Electric Hot Hatch Alpine Should Build
items.summary: Few brands have reinvented themselves as successfully as Alpine. The A290 has already shown that an electric hot hatch can be genuinely exciting, but there may still be room for something even smaller. In this Design Studio feature, we imagine the Alpine A190: a compact performance EV based on the Renault Twingo…
items.content_html:
Few brands have reinvented themselves as successfully as Alpine. The A290 has already shown that an electric hot hatch can be genuinely exciting, but there may still be room for something even smaller. In this Design Studio feature, we imagine the Alpine A190: a compact performance EV based on the Renault Twingo platform, positioned as the spiritual successor to cars like the Twingo GT.

Rather than competing directly with larger hot hatches such as the Vauxhall Corsa GSE, the A190 would target rivals like the Abarth 500e, combining compact dimensions with lightweight engineering, distinctive styling and Alpine's growing reputation for driver-focused electric performance.

As the brand expands beyond a single sports car into a complete range, an accessible entry-level model like this could become the perfect gateway into Alpine ownership, bringing everyday usability and genuine character to one of Europe's smallest electric cars.


Our rendering doesn't attempt to disguise its Twingo roots. Instead, it embraces the compact proportions while introducing a more purposeful Alpine identity through subtle but effective styling changes, including a wider stance, revised bumpers, bespoke lighting details and a sportier overall character.

Rather than an unrealistic fantasy, this feels like a production-ready interpretation of what an entry-level Alpine could become.

With Alpine already using Renault Group's AmpR Small platform for the A290, adapting the same architecture for a smaller, Twingo-based A190 would be a logical and technically achievable next step as the brand continues to expand.

When the second-generation Renault Twingo arrived in 2007, Renault offered one of Europe's most accessible performance line-ups. Buyers could choose the playful Twingo GT, the brilliant Clio Renaultsport 197, the larger Mégane Renaultsport, or even the surprisingly rapid Mégane dCi 175, a diesel hot hatch renowned for its effortless torque.

Three sizes, multiple personalities and every one comfortably below the £20,000 mark when new. Today, the picture is very different. The only true series-production hot hatch within the Renault Group is the Alpine A290, with prices starting above £30,000.

With the next-generation electric Twingo expected to start at around £17,000-£18,000, a compact Alpine A190 could provide the perfect entry point into the brand, recapturing some of the affordability and fun that once made Renault's small performance cars so appealing.


The second-generation Twingo GT proved that a small, affordable hot hatch didn't need huge power to be fun, using a lively 100hp 1.2-litre turbocharged petrol engine. Its successor switched to a rear-engine, rear-wheel-drive layout and a 110hp 0.9-litre turbo, adding a more playful character without sacrificing everyday usability.
 
Our imagined Alpine A190 returns to front-wheel drive, simplifying production and sharing more components with the standard Twingo EV. A 120hp electric motor may sound modest on paper, but it represents around a 50% increase over the regular Twingo EV and Honda Super N, while remaining only a step below the more expensive Abarth 500e.
 
With the Renault 5 using the same 120hp motor from around £22,000, the Twingo's smaller battery could allow Alpine to price an A190 from around £23,000-£24,000, creating a more profitable model while dramatically lowering the cost of joining the Alpine brand.

If the standard A190 represents Alpine's accessible future, our A190 3E concept explores what happens when the engineers are given almost complete freedom. Inspired by the extraordinary Renault 5 Turbo 3E, this wide-bodied, two-door machine pushes the compact Twingo platform close to its limits with aggressive aerodynamics, huge arches and unmistakable motorsport character.

Renault Group's AmpR Small platform is already capable of supporting front-, rear- and even all-wheel drive, making a more extreme flagship technically feasible. Rather than matching the Renault 5 Turbo 3E's £135,000 price tag and 540hp output, an Alpine version could carve out its own niche with around 250-300hp, rear- or all-wheel drive and a price in the high £40,000s.

It would be the modern equivalent of the Clio V6: a halo model designed to grab headlines rather than chase sales.

Whether the A190 itself ever reaches production remains to be seen, but with the platform, powertrains and an affordable electric Twingo already on the way, a compact Alpine feels like one of the brand's most believable opportunities yet.

It would reconnect Alpine with buyers who simply want an affordable, lightweight hot hatch, just as Renault did so successfully two decades ago.

(Image Credits: The New Yardstick)

items.title: MG GO: Our Vision for Britain's Next Affordable Electric Hatchback
items.summary: MG has become one of Britain's fastest-growing car brands, but one gap remains in its expanding electric line-up: a compact hatchback sitting below the MG4. In this Design Studio feature, we imagine the MG GO, an affordable electric supermini positioned as the EV sibling to today's MG3. At around four metres long,…
items.content_html:
MG has become one of Britain's fastest-growing car brands, but one gap remains in its expanding electric line-up: a compact hatchback sitting below the MG4. In this Design Studio feature, we imagine the MG GO, an affordable electric supermini positioned as the EV sibling to today's MG3.

At around four metres long, the MG GO would give MG four hatchbacks spanning roughly 4.0 to 4.4 metres, creating one of Europe's broadest hatchback line-ups - Offering buyers a clear progression from affordable city car to spacious family hatch.

While many manufacturers continue to prioritise SUVs, a value-focused electric hatchback could strengthen MG's reputation for practicality and affordability, taking on rivals such as the Renault 5, Citroën ë-C3 and BYD Dolphin Surf using technology that already exists within SAIC's growing portfolio.

While the MG3 and MG4 Urban use front‑wheel‑drive powertrains, the upcoming MG GO is expected to follow the larger MG4 by adopting a rear‑wheel‑drive electric platform.

MG has yet to confirm its future naming strategy, and the production version could still emerge as the long‑rumoured MG2. But reserving the “2” badge for a B‑segment hatchback would leave little room for a smaller A‑segment model - or even a European version of the Windsor - should MG decide to expand its electric line-up further.


The affordable EV market is becoming one of the most fiercely contested segments in Europe. Just a few years ago, buyers had relatively few choices below £25,000, but today almost every major manufacturer is joining the fight.

Fiat's Grande Panda Electric is already available for under £21,000, while Volkswagen's upcoming ID.Polo is also expected to start between £20,000 and £21,000 once the UK Electric Car Grant is applied.


While higher-spec versions of the MG GO would target the upper end of the segment, it's the entry-level SE that could make the biggest impact. Priced from an estimated £17,995, it would comfortably undercut many of its European rivals while still offering the space and practicality expected of a modern family hatchback.

Our rendering explores how this simpler specification could look, with more understated styling and cost-conscious detailing than the flagship model.


Whether MG ultimately chooses the name GO or MG2, there is a strong business case for a compact electric hatchback sitting beneath the MG4. As SAIC's most successful European brand, MG is central to the group's long-term ambitions on the continent, and a competitively priced supermini could play a major role in attracting first-time EV buyers while strengthening the brand's value-focused reputation.

Recent MG launches have shown that the company is capable of matching established European rivals for technology, practicality and perceived quality, often while undercutting them on price.

If that formula can be applied to a smaller hatchback, the MG GO could quickly become one of the most important affordable EVs in Europe. And with the B-segment electric hot hatch beginning to return, led by models such as the Alpine A290, Peugeot E-208 GTi and Vauxhall Corsa GSe, perhaps there would even be room for an MG GO XPower.

If MG gets the formula right, the GO could become the affordable EV benchmark. And if an XPower version eventually joined the range, it might just become one of the most exciting small electric hot hatchbacks on sale too.

 



(Image Credits: The New Yardstick Design Studio)
